column5: Katz: visualization is a way of finding new visual and narrative ideas before shooting, not a way to remove decisions on set. The storyboard is expected to change once shooting begins. Supports the module 1 framing of visualization as thinking, not a fixed plan.

Katz's analysis questions take a scene through its purpose, what the character wants, what the audience should learn and feel, and then ask what visual choice serves each answer. Use as a worked method in module 1, with an invented scene labelled as illustrative.

Katz advises giving actors an emotional goal and room to find their own process, and keeping technical marks from distracting them. Asks the director to rehearse at about half intensity. Relevant to modules 2 and 3, and useful alongside Norrthon's cueing study.

Katz notes film rehearsal is short, sometimes nonexistent, while stage directors usually get three or four times as much. He suggests marking rooms with masking tape and rehearsing on location. A useful contrast with the theatre sources.

column4: ch-010 identification through sight lines and screen time
column5: Katz explains that a shot's identification depends on sight lines, close-ups and how much screen time each character gets. The viewer tends to side with the character given the most screen time and the clearest sight line. Usable in module 2 on directing performance and point of view.

column4: ch-011 staging patterns A, I and L
column5: Katz's staging system: pattern (A, I or L) decides camera placement along the line of action, and position decides how the actors face within the frame. Ten positions for two actors. A practical vocabulary for module 4.

Katz argues the 180-degree rule is a convention that can be broken on purpose, and cites Ozu's consistent rule-breaking. The course should present the rule as the default with its exceptions, not as a law.

Katz contrasts Welles, who separates characters in deep space (Citizen Kane), with Renoir, who uses movement in depth to make characters meet. Both use depth to show relationships. Relevant to module 4 and module 6 on space.

column4: ch-010 coverage versus cutting in the camera
column5: Katz sets out the trade-off: cutting in the camera risks everything on one take, while coverage is safe but uses up time. He gives the father-dialogue example, where a single dolly shot might be replaced by eight setups. Module 5 on shooting plans.

Katz treats continuity editing as questions and answers between shots, with the cut on the look as the simplest pattern and Kuleshov's experiment as its basis. Usable in module 5 for explaining why a cut works.

column4: ch-009 production design and the art department
column5: Katz explains the art department's role: production designer, art director, illustrators and previs artists, with concept art, plans and continuity sketches in preproduction. Relevant to module 6 on working with designers.
